extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and early-career fiction writers (especially SF/F), conference attendees, and writers building professional networks
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and actionable criteria for networking within the writing industry — how to meet authors, agents, and editors and how to build and sustain a writing-community network (conferences, volunteering, peer groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden networking beyond editors/agents/publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Networking isn’t just getting to know editors, agents, and publishers. It’s also how you relate to the greater community, and how we all build that community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek opportunities to engage with the wider writing community (writing groups, anthologies, conferences) rather than only collecting industry contacts. Value community-building outcomes (collaborations, anthologies, long-term peer relationships).

rubrics_metrics.name: Volunteer to learn and shape the community
rubrics_metrics.description: Volunteering is one of the best ways to network within a community. It allows you to see how things are working and to shape them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volunteer on boards, magazines, conferences, or organizations to meet people, learn processes, and influence how the community operates. Example: the hosts met through volunteering on a magazine and at conferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conferences, retreats, and events as networking hubs
rubrics_metrics.description: Conferences, writing groups, anthologies, and retreats provide valuable networking opportunities at every industry level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend panels, parties, and meetups; these are places where writing groups form, anthologies originate, and long-term professional relationships develop. Focus on interactions that foster sustained contact, not just one-off meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remember names and use techniques to improve recall
rubrics_metrics.description: Remembering names matters; work on tools to make your brain remember people (e.g., look at server name tags, use names in conversation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: observe name tags, use the person's name during conversation, adapt language to avoid awkward phrasing if you’re unsure (e.g., say 'It was good talking to you' instead of 'So nice to meet you'). Acknowledge memory limits and adjust behavior rather than risk micro-aggressing by pretending to remember.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know yourself and network authentically
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t try to imitate other people’s networking style; think about how you normally relate to people and expand on that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify what comes naturally (e.g., small-talk, karaoke, quiet one-on-ones) and scale it to professional settings. Authentic approaches are more sustainable and less draining than forced mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin conversations with common ground and small talk
rubrics_metrics.description: When approaching someone, begin with common ground or small talk — 'small talk exists to basically say, “Hello. I am not a threat.”'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with neutral topics (e.g., weather, panels, venue logistics) to humanize and lower barriers before moving to professional discussion. Steer toward mutual interests if discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize peer networking over chasing famous authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t just chase famous authors; watch for peers too. Peers will grow with you and often provide more long-term value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest time in authors at similar career stages; these relationships can become lifelong and open opportunities (jobs, collaborations, critique groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remember: the work comes first
rubrics_metrics.description: In terms of selling a book, it still comes down to the work; networking won’t replace quality of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use networking to learn about the field and make connections, but ensure your manuscript/portfolio is strong — relationships may help slightly, but not substitute for good writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the 'hierarchy of time' (be mindful of others' time demands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hierarchy of time: how many people want a piece of you affects how valuable your time is; editors and agents often have more people wanting their time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be concise and considerate with agents/editors; contribute to their enjoyment of an interaction rather than monopolizing them. Understand that their time is in high demand and act accordingly (good manners, prepared questions, brevity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay attention to what editors/agents are excited about; let them pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask editors what books they’re working on and what excites them; you’re letting them pitch to you and learning what the field values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use their enthusiasm as a conversation starter and market research—read the books they mention to understand current tastes. This both respects their interests and gives you actionable insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ready to talk business — practice an elevator pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to talk business if they ask. Practice your sales pitch / elevator pitch and know what you are writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a concise, practiced description of your project so you can answer smoothly when asked 'What are you working on?' Avoid halting or vague responses; rehearse a tight logline and a one-sentence hook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribute to others' success — be non-transactional and generous
rubrics_metrics.description: Make genuine friends, don’t just follow task lists; do non-transactional things to help people (signal-boost, donate, beta-read).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice 'five things you can do to help someone without getting credit' (homework): quiet signal boosting, donations, fulfilling wishes, beta reading, referring work. Generosity builds reciprocal goodwill and strengthens the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a conversation makes you uncomfortable, prioritize safety and walk away
rubrics_metrics.description: Networking is great, but your own safety and comfort are important; if something makes you uncomfortable, you can walk away — it won't kill your career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor power dynamics and your emotional comfort; have exit strategies at events. Do not feel obligated to endure harassment or pressure to secure contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use panels and post-panel interactions as natural conversation starters
rubrics_metrics.description: Going to an editor’s panel and approaching them afterward about the panel gives you information and an easy conversation starter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask about points made on the panel, follow up on specifics, and use that shared context to start a more meaningful exchange. Approach at appropriate moments (after panels, at parties) rather than interrupting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend others and spread opportunities when you can’t take work
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can’t take a job, suggest three or four other people; spreading opportunities builds relationships with both peers and hiring editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a mental list of reliable peers to recommend. This generosity signals community orientation and often reciprocates with goodwill and future opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being transactional; cultivate genuine friendships
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be known as the person who’s always looking for who can 'move me up'; be genuinely interested in people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on real curiosity and friendship rather than viewing contacts only as career ladders. Long-term social capital comes from authentic relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware different genres/fields have different social norms
rubrics_metrics.description: The publishing industry is generally friendly in SF/F, but other genres may not be; take that under advisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe the norms of the specific genre community you’re entering and adapt expectations and tactics accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and smooth delivery of your pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice your elevator pitch so that when asked 'So, what are you working on?' you can answer it smoothly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehearse concise, compelling summaries of projects; avoid filler language ('Well. I mean. It’s kind of a…') that undermines credibility. Example: the hosts practiced answering succinctly about 'Ghost Station.'
